The first thing I remember about beginnings is that they don’t feel like beginnings. They feel like ordinary hours that happen to be wearing a costume. A doorbell rings, someone laughs in the kitchen, the kettle begins its small insistence, and then—later—you realize you were living a fork in the road without knowing you’d stepped onto a path that would require you to decide who you were.

People talk about “turning points” as if they arrive with music swelling behind them. In reality, turning points are often mundane. They’re a conversation you almost ignore. They’re a look someone gives you as if they see a version of you that you haven’t learned how to access yet. They’re a late-night decision made from a place of exhaustion, when your future self is already being drafted without your permission.

I’ve always found it strange that we use the word “change” to describe such different things. There’s the kind of change that’s dramatic: a move, a breakup, a new job, a diagnosis, a wedding, an irreversible choice. Then there’s the quieter kind: the way your mind starts noticing certain phrases on signs, the way your taste in music slowly shifts without you feeling the moment you stop liking what you used to love. Quiet change is less like a storm and more like a glacier. It moves. It doesn’t announce itself.

Maybe that’s why we underestimate time. We live as if time is a line that will eventually run out, when in fact it behaves more like a river that keeps reorganizing the landscape around us. You can’t hold it. You can only learn to navigate with what it’s giving you. Some days it gives you a smooth current—everything flows. Other days it turns shallow and rocky, and you have to learn how to step differently. The water keeps going either way.

When I think about what makes a life feel meaningful, I don’t picture grand monuments. I picture repetition. I picture the small rituals that help your body trust that the world is stable enough to take comfort in: morning tea, a familiar route, the way you fold a blanket, the act of writing something down even when no one will ever read it. Meaning isn’t only found in moments of triumph. Sometimes it’s found in the decision to keep showing up, again and again, in a way that says, “I’m still here. I’m still paying attention.”

There’s also the question of attention itself. Attention feels like a personal resource, but it’s also social. It’s negotiated between you and everything around you: notifications, obligations, the expectations other people carry. In a world that constantly asks for your gaze, choosing where you place your attention is one of the most intimate choices you can make. You can spend your attention trying to earn someone’s approval. You can spend it trying to outrun your own fears. Or you can spend it on what helps you become more awake to your actual life.

I’ve noticed that fear often masquerades as practicality. It offers you reasons that sound sensible: “If you do this, you’ll fail.” “If you change, everything will collapse.” “If you want something too much, you’ll look foolish.” Fear can dress itself in the language of caution. It can even sound like wisdom. But the tell is that fear usually makes you smaller. It narrows your horizons until your life feels like a corridor you can’t leave.

Hope can be quieter than fear, which means we sometimes don’t recognize it as it arrives. Hope doesn’t always glow. Sometimes it looks like a commitment to keep learning. Sometimes it looks like saying yes to a small risk. Sometimes it looks like caring about something that won’t pay you back quickly. Hope can be a kind of stubbornness—an insistence that your life is not only what has happened to you, but also what you do next.

The strangest part about being human is how much we want to be understood. We want someone to look at our choices and say, “I see why you did that.” Not as an excuse, not as absolution—just as recognition. Recognition is rare. People are busy, and they interpret what they see through the lens of their own stories. Still, when it happens, it feels like warmth. It feels like a hand on the shoulder that says, “You’re not alone in the way you’re trying to survive.”

Solitude, though, can also be medicine. Not the lonely kind that traps you, but the chosen kind that gives you space to hear yourself. There’s a difference between being alone and being lonely. One is the presence of your own thoughts; the other is the absence of connection. In solitude, you can rummage through your mind like a drawer you forgot was there. You can find old ideas that still work. You can throw away habits that no longer fit. You can discover what you believe when you aren’t performing your beliefs for an audience.

Of course, the world keeps insisting on performance. We perform competence at work. We perform stability in relationships. We perform optimism in public. Sometimes we perform grief in the ways expected of us, as if sorrow were a badge worn at the right angle. But beneath performance is a raw person: a collection of needs, memories, and unspoken questions. The more honest we are with ourselves about that rawness, the more compassion we can extend outward.

Compassion is not just a mood. It’s a decision. It’s the practice of imagining that another person’s inner life has its own weather system. You don’t know what storms they’re navigating. You don’t know what past lesson shaped their behavior. You can see the effect of their choices, but not always the full cause. Compassion doesn’t mean tolerating harm. It doesn’t mean ignoring your own boundaries. It means refusing to treat other people like puzzles you can solve through judgment alone.

I used to think wisdom arrived in adulthood like a gift you unwrap. Now I suspect wisdom is more like a slow accumulation of repair work. We learn that our first interpretations were incomplete. We learn that being right isn’t the same as being kind. We learn that certainty can be a trap. We learn that people change—not always in the ways we hope, but in ways they are capable of. We learn that sometimes the best thing you can do is not to force an outcome, but to become the kind of person who can handle multiple outcomes without collapsing.

There’s also the question of joy. Joy is often treated like a reward, something you earn after you clear the obstacles. But joy is more like oxygen. It doesn’t replace the work of your life; it accompanies it. It shows up in small, almost embarrassing places: the smell of rain through an open window, the sudden clarity of a line of poetry, the feeling of your body relaxing after a long day, the way laughter travels through a room like a bright signal.

When you stop waiting for joy to become “proper,” you begin to notice it more. You begin to see it as evidence that you’re still alive, still capable of delight. And that matters, because a life without delight can turn into mere endurance. Endurance is necessary, sometimes. But life is not only endurance. Life is also discovery.

I don’t know what the right answer is to how to live. If there were a single recipe, people would have it by now, and the world would be less confusing. But maybe the point is that living is the recipe. You taste as you go. You adjust. You learn from what doesn’t work. You forgive yourself for being unfinished.

In the end, perhaps the most honest thing you can say about your own life is this: you are a work in progress moving through time, carrying a body, holding relationships, making choices with imperfect information. You will be hurt. You will hurt others sometimes, even unintentionally. You will also love, and you will also be loved, in ways you may not recognize at first.

If beginnings don’t announce themselves, then maybe the task is to keep your senses open. To pay attention to the ordinary hours wearing costumes. To notice when you’re being asked—quietly—to become someone braver, gentler, more awake. And when that moment comes, to respond as best you can, even if you don’t know what it will lead to.

Because whatever comes next—whatever story your life starts to write—will be made out of the same substance as everything you’ve already lived: time, attention, choice, and the small, stubborn act of continuing.
